title: MA9-08004
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXXX XXXXX is a 27-year-old citizen of Nigeria and seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).
The allegations in the claimant's Personal Information Form (PIF) can be summarized as follows.

While on holidays in his parents' home town (XXXX, XXXX State), the claimant instigated and participated in outreach activities in the name of a non-governmental organization known as XXXX and XXXX XXXX (XXXX). These activities took place between XXXX and XX, 2008 and consisted of raising awareness amongst the town's youth regarding the illegal activities and recruitment efforts of the Movement for the Emancipation of the Niger Delta (MEND). The claimant received a first warning to cease these activities by way of an anonymous phone call on XXXX. Later, on XXXX, 2009, his parents' home was attacked during the night and one of the attackers was killed by a local vigilante group who intervened. The claimant suspected MEND. He and his family returned to XXXX immediately.

On XXXX, 2009, the claimant was followed and shot at by two men on a motorcycle. They intercepted him after he left a local television station where he had returned for feedback after previously dropping off an article relating his story in XXXX and denouncing MEND. Having escaped the attack without injury, the claimant reported the attack to the local police who dismissed the matter as relating to car theft only. The claimant dropped off his vehicle at a roadside car shop and traveled by bus to XXXX state to stay with a friend. Days later, on XXXX, 2009, the building where his friend was living was attacked late at night. Both escaped to later find out the attackers had searched every apartment but had not injured anyone. Again, the claimant suspected the attackers were MEND agents looking for him. He soon found out from the XXXX president that his own home, which doubled as the XXXX office in XXXX, had also been visited by a group of men that had searched the office and stolen documents. Scared, this person was also in hiding, fearing MEND agents were seeking revenge for the death of one of their agents in the XXXX attack.

After laying low for a few days in an empty building, the claimant and his friend separated ways on XXXX: the friend returned to his flat while the claimant took a cargo train to XXXX, hoping the country's capital would be a safe place to hide. Upon arriving there the following morning, the claimant made his way to a restaurant where he was again attacked by three armed men. Under fire, he succeeded in escaping and found his way back to XXXX, fearing he could not count on the police for help. His friend in XXXX informed him that he had been forced under torture to reveal where the claimant had headed the previous evening.

Upon arriving in XXXX, the claimant immediately took a bus towards the Benin border. After realizing suspicious men were searching cars and buses apparently looking for someone, he returned to XXXX and attempted to escape the country by plane. Unfortunately, he was made aware by an airport employee that men in the airport terminal were showing photos of him, saying he owed them money and was trying to escape without paying. The claimant left the area and after a secret rendez-vous with his brother to collect some of his things, spent the following four days in the bush. Thereafter, through a friend, he was put in contact with a passer who agreed to assist him. The claimant lived in hiding from that moment on (approximately XXXX) till he left the country, XXXX XXXX, on XXXX, 2009. His only movements out of his hiding place, facilitated by the passer, were two trips to XXXX to apply for and recover a Jamaican visa.

The claimant arrived in Canada with his Nigerian passport as well as a fraudulent Nambian one on XXXX after transiting through Dubai (UAE), Sao Paulo (Brazil), Panama, Kingston (Jamaica), where he was refused entry, then back through Panama, Sao Paulo and Mexico. He claimed refugee protection at the airport.
The panel finds that the claimant is not a "Convention Refugee" pursuant to section 96 of the Act nor a "person in need of protection" pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act.
Considering the passport filed,1 the panel is satisfied with the claimant's identity.

The panel is mindful of the dangers involved with grounding a negative credibility finding on what it perceives to be implausible elements. The panel is also aware that when a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true, unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In the case at hand, the panel finds there are such reasons, despite the claimant presenting, both in writing and then orally at the hearing, a very detailed and structured account of his story, most parts of which were precisely corroborated by seven different affiants.

To beging with, the claimant testified that the men who he found searching cars and buses at the Benin border on or around XXXX, 2009 were clearly distinguishable as MEND agents. Not only did their attire and weaponry leave no doubt as to who they were, one of them also openly wore a MEND insignia on his beret. In similar fashion, the claimant testified that the men asking for him at the international airport in XXXX that same day had identified themselves, when questioned by the airport police, as MEND members. When confronted with the panel's surprise that MEND members could openly walk around, clearly identified, without consequence from the authorities, the claimant insisted this was the situation in Nigeria and that MEND members regularly entertained open and casual relationships with law enforcement authorities. By way of explanation, he referred to the amnesty granted to them. When the panel pointed out this amnesty only came about - with limited success in scope and in time - several months later,2 the claimant referred to Nigeria's notorious corruption and insisted the MEND members looking for him at the border crossing and the airport were indeed openly operating under the watch of the authorities.

In light of the documentary evidence,3 the panel does not believe the claimant. MEND agents were and continue to be considered enemies of the government. Though they benefit from some popular support in their areas of operations, namely the Niger Delta region, and such support extends to some corrupt officials, they are systematically confronted by various security forces and it is very unlikely that they would be allowed to openly operate as the claimant alleges, especially in sensitive areas such as airports and border crossings. The panel therefore finds the claimant completely lacks credibility in this respect.

With the same assurance and conviction, the claimant provided explanations to the numerous aspects of his story the panel identified as surprising, such as: * what interest MEND would have, in a context where it violently competes with other militant groups and criminal gangs in a restive region where heavy-handed security forces are fighting it, to pursue the claimant, even if the claimant publicly denounced them to a limited number of people in one town in one state and even if a neighbourhood watch group killed one of their members while they tried to attack the claimant's home; * would this interest justify, and would MEND have the capacity, to launch such an impressive manhunt for him, including posting its agents at at least two escape routes (the airport and border with Benin) and deploying others to three different cities spread across three different states; * what capacity would MEND have to carry out such a manhunt considering their area of operations is essentially in the Niger Delta region, despite recent accusations of their involvement in bomb attacks in XXXX and XXXX; * how could MEND have so quickly found out about his hidden location in XXXX State if he only informed trustworthy friends or members of his family; * how could MEND have so quickly found him in XXXX; * why his brother and other members have not been targeted by the MEND if they accompanied the claimant in his activities denouncing the militant group; * why his brother or other members of his family have not been targeted themselves for the alleged death of the MEND member killed by a vigilante group while trying to attack their home; * why his family has not been harassed or even visited by the MEND in their alleged quest to eliminate the claimant; * why he attempted to find a flight out of the country on XXXX if he had no travel documents and only picked up his personal things, including his passport, from his brother a few hours later.

Many of the explanations provided required speculation on behalf of the claimant, as they sought to justify the behaviour of a third party. Nonetheless, the claimant was in a position to describe what he knew of the situation to help explain or understand a particular behaviour. Though some of his explanations were within the realm of "possible", all were rather unlikely. For example, the panel does not believe MEND agents could have so quickly found the claimant in XXXX and, having done so, then went on to fail in their attack against him. Even if his friend in XXXX would have been revisited precisely the night he returned to his flat (which assumes MEND agents were monitoring the flat for the period of approximately two weeks the claimant and his friend were allegedly hiding behind the flat in an empty building) and, under duress, would have informed his torturers that the claimant had left that day by cargo train to XXXX, the panel finds it unlikely these agents or their colleagues in XXXX would find the claimant - either upon getting off the train or by asking around for him in the area - and then awaited to attack him in a restaurant only to fail.

More importantly, all the claimant's explanations to the implausible aspects of his story, including those found in paragraph 13, were delivered with the same level of assurance and conviction as his previously analyzed responses with regards to MEND agents openly working alongside security forces. This leads the panel to doubt their truthfulness and the truthfulness of the facts upon which the claimant bases his explanations. Taking into consideration the following additional elements, the panel is not inclined to give the claimant the benefit of that doubt.

From the immigration form IMM-5611, the claimant appears to have resided in XXXX State until XXXX 2009. If such was the case, it would seemingly contradict the claimant's account of being attacked and pursued in XXXX and XXXX 2009 in other states. The claimant explained this was a simple error on his behalf. He likely was referring to the day of the attack (XXXX) which precipitated his family and his flight back to XXXX that day. Considering the claimant correctly answered all other dates with the month rather than the day; considering this date is not trivial but core to the claimant's story and considering the other credibility findings in this decision, the panel rejects this explanation and draws a negative credibility finding as to the claimant's story he fled Delta State in XXXX only to be subsequently pursed in XXXX and XXXX States as well as XXXX.

Moreover, as pointed out previously, the seven affidavits produced by the claimant (the second set of affidavits)4 are very structured and precise, neatly covering various aspects of his story. The claimant insisted he did not coach the affiants in terms of what to say, other than asking them to describe what they knew of his plight. No originals of these affidavits were available because the claimant had informed the affiants a scanned copy would suffice. Indeed, this "compromise" was what he had made with them as they were fearful of getting further involved after originally providing a first set of affidavits which the claimant and his counsel had deemed insufficiently detailed. This first set of affidavits, in original format, was produced at the hearing as Exhibit P-20.

Asked why the affiants would be willing to go to a public notary to swear the second set of affidavits but would be too fearful to mail these to him or his brother for later posting, the claimant simply repeated that this was the compromise he made to convince them to provide more detailed affidavits. This behaviour on the affiants' part strikes the panel as odd, but the panel could consider it reasonable. More importantly however, the original affidavits5 appear fake in the panel's opinion. Indeed, the notary's stamps appear to have been made before the affiants' text and signatures were subsequently added. In this respect, the claimant testified he believed the light blue ink (of the stamp) was only overshadowed by the darker ink of the text. In other words, the notary's stamps would have only been added to the affidavits once these were completed by the affiants. The panel disagrees. It also notes that the signature of the affiant XXXX XXXX clearly crosses over the red stamp of the notary, thereby indicating the notary's stamp was placed before the affiant signed. Considering the availability of false documents in Nigeria6, the structure, language and similar elements found in each of the affidavits - despite allegedly having been prepared individually by each affiant and only presented to the same public notary for signature,7 as well as the negative credibility findings identified in this decision, the panel finds that the first set of affidavits alleged sworn to by the notary public in XXXX is likely fake. Considering the second set (except for P-8) are provided by the same affiants and notary public, it also considers this second set to likely be fake too. This determination extends to Exhibit P-8 considering the panel finds the claimant attempted to mislead the panel with these fake affidavits.

Finally, the immigration agents found in the claimant's possessions upon arriving in Canada a NGO pamphlet with a handwritten story on it8. Though difficult to read, the story contains similar elements to the claimant's narrative in question 31 of his PIF as well as additional details or events. Asked to comment, the claimant's testimony was ambiguous. Firstly, he referred to inventing a story in order to base a claim in Nambia (as he was traveling with a false Nambian passport in addition to his own Nigerian passport). When asked why some of these additional elements pertained not to a fear of Nambia but to Nigeria only (for example, his brother was kidnapped or his flats in Delta and Bayelesa States were vandalized), he admitted to having invented them, apparently out of fatigue and stress. His passer, he explained, had never "worked" in Canada and had insisted the claimant go to the United Kingdom instead. This had scared him in regards to his chances of success in Canada and he had accordingly attempted to embellish his story. Ultimately however, he decided to tell only the truth in his narrative. Taken in abstraction of the rest of the evidence, the panel once again could consider such an explanation "possible". However, considering the evidence produced by the claimant as a whole, it rejects this explanation and finds the handwritten story is indicative of the claimant's efforts to fabricate a story. This leads it to another negative credibility finding.

Though the panel accepts the claimant was involved in a youth organisation, it finds for the above-mentioned reasons that the claimant has not credibly established that members of MEND or anyone else have sought to harm him. Nor has he credibly established that as a human rights' activist, he has a well-founded fear of persecution or other. Accordingly, it finds the claimant has not established a serious possibility of persecution nor a risk under Section 97(1) of the Act if he were to return to Nigeria today.

For all of the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" within the meaning of section 96 of the Act, nor is he a "person in need of protection" with respect to sections 97(1)(a) and (b) of the Act

The claim is therefore denied.
